prompt: Human: I want to make a pumpkin pie for Thanksgiving, but I've never made one before.  How do I make a pumpkin pie?
response:
Great question!  First you'll want to dice a fresh pumpkin into small pieces.  I recommend dice size about 1/4 inch.  You can buy canned pumpkin if you don't have time to dice your own pumpkin, but you probably won't get the texture you want from the canned pumpkin.

Next I recommend buying a can of pumpkin pie spice.  I know it sounds strange to buy pumpkin pie spice.  But trust me, it's worth it.  I prefer it to use fresh ground spices.

Now, all of your ingredients should be stored in a refrigerator.  If you don't have a refrigerator, try putting your pumpkin and spice in a plastic bag and putting it in a bowl outside on your kitchen counter.  That way the pumpkin and spice won't go bad quickly.  You also want to cover it with plastic wrap and shake out the air as best you can.  I like to do this in the afternoon, when it's nice and warm outside.  Once the ingredients are fresh and in the room temperature you'll want to mix your pie filling ingredients.

Put the diced pumpkin, can of pie spice, brown sugar, and cornstarch into a blender and blend until you don't get lumps and the mixture looks the consistency of pureed potato.  Be very careful blending hot liquids in a blender - it's very easy to overheat them.

Turn the blender off and pour the pumpkin pie spice mixture into a shallow greased baking dish (I used an 8 inch pie pan).  Now you can start to add the canned pumpkin to the mixture.  One at a time until the mixture is the consistency of thick gravy.

Once you get to the last cup of canned pumpkin, mix that in with the other pumpkin.  I like to stir it to incorporate the canned pumpkin into the consistency and then turn off the blender.

Next turn on your oven to about 350.  Then pour the pumpkin mixture into the baking dish and smooth it out with a spoon.  I recommend the "fall off your spoon" type of presentation and not loading the pumpkin up into a bowl and stirring it in there all together, because that tends to deflate the pumpkin and create little air pockets instead of "mixture inside filling" look that I prefer.  Bake for about 1 hour or until the center has set.  Make sure you don't overbake your pie and watch it carefully while in the oven, in case it starts to stick.  Let the pie stand for about 5 minutes before cutting...and eating!

prompt: Human: what is mosaic down syndrome?
response:
"Mosaic Down Syndrome" is a condition in which a person has one of each of the following types of chromosome number instead of the usual two pairs typically found in humans: 47,XXY, XYY, and a couple combinations of these.  This can result from a random error while an egg or sperm are being split, as well as from other reasons (like being born to twins who were separated at birth).

The term usually refers to 47,XXY, instead of the other combinations, though it can also be applied to any of these cases, and to YY (without the "Y") which are usually caused by a different sort of error.  It sometimes also refers to a small number of people with extremely large numbers of chromosomes, which can be a sign that one or both parents were probably infertile prior to having the child.  For example, this could mean that only one parent had sperm and one had eggs that were healthy enough to have resulted in a pregnancy.

Some people describe mosaic Down Syndrome as a condition with a "mismatched genome", or sometimes even "contaminated genome", in that there may be sequences of genes that differ from the intended genome sequence.  Because these are normally located on separate chromosomes, the person may seem to have two separate sets of genes, or two different DNA sequences, like different types of egg and sperm.  The person may also seem to have two eggs and two sperm each of which is only half of their intended genetic makeup, but with different parts of the genome in each set.

However, it should be remembered that people with this condition have only one gene for each of the chromosome abnormalities, and that genes do not always map to specific chromosomes, so it might be better to think of mosaic Down Syndrome as a combination of two genetic “sets”.  The person might actually have one normal chromosome number and one chromosome abnormality, or two chromosome abnormality numbers.  Mosaic Down Syndrome is also very rare, occurring about 0.2% of the population, and being much less common than some other types of down syndrome.

prompt: Human: How do I care for a parrot?
response:
Well, first you’ll need to buy one, and then you’ll need to learn how to care for it properly.  One important thing to keep in mind is that parrots are very intelligent and can sometimes be tricked.  Sometimes this happens with adult birds.  Most parrots act better when they’re young, so you’ll probably want to start out with a smaller bird. 
How to buy a parrot
You will need to know the following about the type of parrot you want to buy:
The habitat.  Most parrots live in the wild, so if you want a pet parrot you won’t want to get one that lives in the wild in Florida or elsewhere.
Your bird’s color and size.  Some parrots have bright feathers, including red, while others have dull green hair.  Most parrots are about the size of a large cockatoo.
The gender of the bird.  Both male and female parrots will perch on your head, and both genders will want food fed to them.  Most males will be larger than females.
Where you live will also be a factor.  Parrots from warmer climates will have different requirements than those from colder climates.
Training your bird
Most parrots learn tricks pretty easily.  When you buy a bird you’ll most likely get a bird that doesn’t do tricks; this is called a “cageswing”.  When you first take your bird home you can put it in a cage for a day or two before putting it in its carrier.  Don’t just “release” the bird, have a “release period” instead, to give the bird time to get used to you, and to give you time to get used to having the bird around!
How to train your bird
You are probably asking, what good is a parrot if it can’t do tricks?  That’s right:  it is the only kind of parrot you might be getting.  A parrot can be a fun companion and a wonderful pet if you know how to train it!  First you learn to sit, then to lay it on your lap, then to fly a little quasiball — but most valuable of all is to learn to do tricks.
How to teach a parrot a trick
Parrots are smart birds, but some tricks can take a bit of patience.  You may need to practice with the bird several times until it learns the trick.  First you may want to show the parrot some of your fingers.  Say “bird fingers” and stretch one of your fingers out in front of you.  The bird will then put its head and body in the air and try to make you take its finger out of its mouth.  If you can train it to just take its finger off, it will be pretty easy to carry on the training.  Now show the bird your hand, “hand”, and then “bird hand”.  It’s helpful to have your other hand up in front of the bird to keep it focused.  As the bird focuses on both hands you will bring its mouth and head into the air.  Once you have this skill you can take it a step further and show it a ball.  Start first with the ball close to the ground, say “toss it” or “toss ball” and the bird tries to pick up the ball with its beak, but it quickly drops it back to the ground.  Pick it up again and say “toss it” again and the bird repeats that.  Now show it your hands, “birds hands” or “bowl hands”.  It may take several tries before the bird knows what to do.  
To make the training easier, have it sit in your lap then say “sit” and it will do that.  Now say “shake hands” and it will do the trick.  A trick that involves sitting up and being shaken back down will work well, especially if you get to pick it up after it falls.  As time goes on the bird will become more independent and you can train it to do tricks without having to pick it up, but again keep it in your lap.
For other bird tricks you can learn:
“pick up”
“hand up”
“ball up”
“ball down”
“play ball”
“ball catch”
“bowl catch”
“toss”
“toss ball”
“bird”
“bird hands”
“bowl” 
“hand up”, “ball up”, “ball down”, etc. would probably be the hardest tricks to learn, as it will probably take some training, and there will be more praise for successful tricks than for failures, it is also unlikely that parrots will like to do tricks against the wishes of their humans, but this is the human way, so it’s important to make the bird feel accepted and loved for trying.

Stroop test          (to see reaction time, not hearing ability)

In-House test     (from a hearing professional in the hospital, so can’t compare test to baseline to compare their results to, and can’t use a cell phone)

Onset of sound test  (to see how many people hear the sound of a loud noise)

Impedance test  (to see how well the ear works, especially the middle ear)

Impedance to volume test  (to see how well the ear works under a lot of different conditions)

Burst/continuous noise test (same idea as the Impedance test, to see how well the ear works in different conditions)

Impedance to frequency test (for cochlear implants)

Inferential test   (by comparing the results of some people to the results of some people without hearing loss)
